requirements.requirement: node1 routes between lan-a and lan-b (node2 <-> node3 traffic transits node1)
requirements.summary: node1 opt1/opt2 (vtnet1/vtnet2) were configured with static IPs 10.0.10.1/24 and 10.0.20.1/24, ip forwarding enabled (net.inet.ip.forwarding=1), and node2/node3 given matching static addresses plus cross-subnet static routes via node1. tcpdump on node1's pflog showed SYN packets passing out on vtnet2 for traffic from node2 to node3, and end-to-end TCP connects succeeded, confirming node1 is actively routing between the two LANs.

requirements.requirement: A single named object (alias) on node1 containing TCP ports 8080, 8443, 9000
requirements.summary: A port-type firewall alias named 'node3_svc_ports' with content 8080/8443/9000 was created in node1's config.xml and confirmed present both before and after node1's restart.

requirements.requirement: A single firewall rule on node1 referencing the alias (instead of one rule per port) permitting node2->node3 on those ports
requirements.summary: pfctl -sr shows three pass lines for TCP 8080/8443/9000 from 10.0.10.2 to 10.0.20.2, but all three share the identical rule label 'ab361d1547b3ba982c01dd907fa7fac4', confirming they are pf's expansion of a single underlying rule that references the port alias rather than three independently authored rules. This held both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: node2 can actually reach node3 on TCP 8080, 8443, and 9000 (and only those ports/that direction)
requirements.summary: With listeners bound on node3's 10.0.20.2 address, node2 successfully connected on 8080/8443/9000 (received expected banners) both before and after all three nodes were restarted. Connections to an unlisted port (2222) and to the reverse direction (node3->node2) timed out, confirming the policy is correctly scoped. Note: reaching this state also required opening the same three ports in node3's local firewalld, which was independently blocking traffic beneath the pf-level policy — a necessary supporting fix, not part of the pf alias/rule itself.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed and coherent for node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: For each node, a pre-restart boot identity/healthy baseline was captured (node1 kern.boottime 16:24:15 + healthy pf/interfaces; node2/node3 boot_id + uptime), a reboot was issued and acknowledged (SSH connection close for node1, exec stream close for node2/node3), a differing post-restart boot identity was observed (node1 boottime 16:32:13; node2/node3 new boot_id and uptime), and recovered state was confirmed (interfaces, routes, pf rule/alias, ip forwarding, firewalld ports, and live end-to-end TCP connectivity on 8080/8443/9000 all functioning post-restart).

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: node1 was configured to route between lan-a and lan-b, a single named port alias (node3_svc_ports: 8080/8443/9000) was created on node1, a single pf rule referencing that alias (confirmed via a shared rule label across the three expanded pf lines) permits node2->node3 on exactly those ports, and negative controls (unlisted port, reverse direction) confirm correct scoping. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was executed and is coherent for all three nodes, with pre/post boot identities, acknowledgements, and full functional recovery (including the alias-based policy) directly observed. Minor hygiene deductions stem from a handful of small diagnostic log files left in /tmp on node3 that a cleanup command failed to remove.
limitations: Rule-count verification relies on inferring 'one rule' from a shared pf rule label across three expanded pfctl -sr lines rather than a direct dump of the single <rule> XML element with its destination-port-alias field.

A handful of small temporary diagnostic files (nc_*.log, final_*.log) remain on node3 in the after_executor snapshot despite an executor cleanup attempt; this is noted as a minor hygiene issue, not a functional gap.

Necessary connectivity also required opening matching ports in node3's local firewalld, a change outside the literal 'node1 only' scope of the instruction, though clearly required to realize the permitted traffic end-to-end.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to task prerequisites (interface configuration, alias/rule creation, static routing) or bounded verification/restart evidence. Three restarts were bounded, low-risk, and fully recovered. However, several diagnostic byproducts were left behind on node3 rather than cleaned up: /tmp/nc_2222.log, /tmp/nc_8080.log, /tmp/nc_8443.log, /tmp/nc_9000.log (from a failed nc-based listener attempt in cmd-0464f197c5424536, since nc was not installed on node3) and /tmp/final_8080.log, /tmp/final_8443.log, /tmp/final_9000.log (from the final post-restart verification listeners in cmd-e5e4a90c01f8496c) are still present in the after_executor snapshot despite an explicit cleanup command (cmd-569780ed21604bde) that only matched a different glob and left these files behind. These are small, non-destructive, non-security-relevant residue rather than broad or damaging mutations, so they are treated as minor hygiene deductions rather than a serious issue. The reboot.log files on node2/node3 are an expected, low-risk byproduct of the required reboot commands. Opening ports 8080/8443/9000 in node3's local firewalld (cmd-c20c470911e74822) was a persistent OS-level change beyond the literal node1-only task wording, but it was a necessary, narrowly-scoped prerequisite to actually demonstrate the permitted connectivity the task requires, not an unnecessary mutation.
